A 3-year-old boy weighing 12 kg was brought to the emergency department 1 hour after an alleged ingestion of approximately 10 mL of a 12.5% amitraz solution. On arrival, he was dull and only responsive to tactile stimuli. His pulse rate was 59 beats/min, and his systolic blood pressure was 60 mmHg. He received 0.6 mg of intravenous atropine, after which his heart rate rose to 134 beats/min and his blood pressure to 82/44 mmHg. He was transferred to the intensive care unit, where he was noted to be obtunded with bilateral pinpoint pupils; the remainder of the examination was unremarkable. Arterial blood gas analysis showed a pH of 7.24, a PCO2 of 65 mmHg, and a PO2 of 105 mmHg, consistent with acute respiratory acidosis. He was immediately intubated and started on assisted ventilation. Routine laboratory studies were within normal limits.

A 7-year-old girl presented with a 2-year history of an enlarging, intermittently painful, purplish lump in her left ear canal. Approximately 18 months earlier, she had developed cracking and pus-filled sores at the site and received antibiotics and analgesics before referral. On examination, there was a 3.5 × 2.5 cm purplish-red mass in the left external ear canal, with an irregular, friable surface and bleeding on minimal contact. Contrast-enhanced CT of the mastoids showed a lobulated mass in the cutis and subcutis of the left auricle extending into the external acoustic canal and into the left parotid space, with bilateral level II–IV cervical lymph nodes up to 0.6 cm in diameter. CT angiography demonstrated marked vascularity of the mass, supplied by branches of the left superficial temporal and posterior auricular arteries. Incisional biopsy revealed atypical cells and granulomatous inflammation, leading to a provisional diagnosis of an auricular malignant tumor without a clear histopathological subtype.

A 62-year-old woman presented with a one-month history of burning sensation and discomfort in her left breast without fever or systemic symptoms. She had hypertension and a remote history of hemorrhoidectomy, dilation and curettage, colonoscopy, and gastroscopy; she was a heavy smoker. On examination, there was a 3 × 3 cm palpable mass in the upper quadrant of the left breast without overlying skin changes. No axillary or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy was noted. Routine blood tests, chest radiograph, and ECG were unremarkable. Breast MRI revealed an ill-defined, deep retroareolar spiculated lesion measuring 3 × 1.5 cm with an early enhancement peak and associated architectural distortion; no axillary lymphadenopathy or skin thickening was identified (BIRADS IV). An excisional biopsy showed breast tissue containing cohesive nests of neoplastic epithelial cells within a dense lymphoid infiltrate. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated that the epithelial cells were positive for cytokeratin AE1/E3 and negative for estrogen receptor, progesterone receptor, and HER2/neu; the background lymphocytes stained positive for CD3 and CD20.

A 9-year-old boy was referred with left cheek swelling and hyperglobus of the left eye. Hyperglobus was first noted about 1 year earlier under ophthalmologic observation. Six months later, swelling of the left cheek developed, with marked progression over the preceding 3 months. 

On extraoral examination, there was a painless, bony-hard swelling of the left cheek. The overlying skin was normal, but the patient reported numbness of the left cheek and weakness in movement of the left upper lip. There were no other neurologic deficits, no visual disturbances, and ocular motility was intact. Intraoral examination revealed expansion of the left maxillary ridge with mobility of primary teeth c, d, and e.

A panoramic radiograph and cone-beam computed tomography demonstrated a large, well-circumscribed, expansile, heterogeneous (mixed-density) mass occupying the entire left maxillary sinus. The lesion caused deviation and destruction of the nasal septum, invaded the ethmoid sinus, thinned, displaced, and perforated the anterior wall of the sphenoid sinus, extended into the pterygopalatine fossa with destruction of the pterygoid plates, and elevated and perforated the left infraorbital rim. There was extreme postero-superior displacement of the second molar toward the inferior orbital fissure, resulting in blockage of the fissure, and compromise of the nasopharyngeal space.

Medical history was notable for seasonal allergic reactions and glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency; blood pressure was documented as 10/5 mmHg. Coagulation studies were within normal limits. Laboratory evaluation showed WBC 19 × 10³/μl, RBC 3.66 × 10⁶/μl, hemoglobin 10.6 g/dl, hematocrit 33.2%, and MCHC 31.9 g/dl; other serum chemistries were normal.

An intraoral incisional biopsy was performed under local anesthesia with mepivacaine to minimize the risk of methemoglobinemia.

The mass had gradually enlarged, was hard in texture, non-tender, and mobile. On examination, a 4.5 × 5.5 cm irregular, poorly defined, hard mass was palpable at the 1 o’clock position in the right breast, 2.5 cm from the nipple, with overlying ulceration and slight serosanguinous discharge. The lesion was fairly mobile without palpable axillary or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy. The left breast was normal.

Breast ultrasound and MRI both classified the lesion as BI-RADS category V. Chest CT demonstrated a right breast mass suggestive of malignancy. Serum breast tumor markers were within normal limits.

A 40-year-old man from eastern India presented with a nonhealing ulcer on the tongue present for the last 4 months. The lesion started as a small painless mass on the right lateral aspect of the tongue, which gradually grew and subsequently ulcerated. It caused mild difficulty in eating. No history of trauma or tongue bite preceding the lesion. Patient denied consuming tobacco or alcohol regularly. Medical history includes well-controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus for 2 years with oral hypoglycemic agents. No systemic complaints. No history of high-risk behavior for HIV.
